newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria economic "Vision" plan faces military test.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria economic "Vision" plan faces military test.

text.p: The eighth session of a Nigerian economic think tank working on a blueprint for the next century drew to a close on Thursday, and some members raised fears that the military rulers may not heed the outcome.
"People have such fears, and I will be deceiving you if I say these fears are not shared by even some of the members of the committee," Vision 2010 secretary Alhaji Ibrahim Ida told Reuters.

"I think the bottom line is the committee was given a task and is doing it in the best way it can ... If they (the government) had no intention of doing what it said then they would not have set up the committee."

The "Vision 2010" Committee, proposed by head of state General Sani Abacha, is charged with delivering a detailed plan in September to carry Nigeria into a 21st Century brighter than the closing years of this one.

The plan gained much of its momentum from the private sector and is headed by Ernest Shonekan, an industrialist and keen supporter of liberalising reforms, who as head of state was toppled by Abacha in 1993.
But the committee of over 200 also has room for some of Nigeria's most conservative figures, among them traditional rulers and others whose interests are to minimise change.

"Bringing some of these people on board to understand the need for change is a major achievement, it is one we hope will be respected," said one Lagos-based banker. "Whether it will be respected only the military can answer ... It's the same as with democracy, nobody really knows."

Abacha, vilified by pro-democracy campaigners and some Western governments, has promised to restore civilian rule in 1998, under a programme many opponents see as a ruse to keep critics at bay while maintaining the military in power.

Since independence from Britain in 1960, successive governments have developed grandiose plans for Africa's most populous nation, funding a bloated state sector and subsidies with oil money that often vanished through waste or corruption.
The oil export-dependent economy was given its greatest knock by the protests and strikes that followed the annulment of 1993 elections by a former military government.
Tight fiscal policies under Abacha appear to have crushed inflation and stabilised the naira currency.

But the tightness of the policies runs to the extent of not even having approved 1997 capital expenditure, let alone released funds, and Nigerian economists see no end to recession unless growth is stimulated through spending or reform.

The 1997 annual budget was a disappointment to many in the private sector, as well as the World Bank, who had expected a strong commitment to privatisation of state enterprises, and the abolition of dual exchange rates.

"What it boils down to is that when the core of those in power decide their interests are threatened,they just draw in their horns and say 'no more'," said one oil company official. "The worry is the same could happen to Vision 2010."
